power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: Experiment 1 used a between-participants design with a factor of the viewing condition (kawaii or objective). For mood outcomes, time (pre-or post-task) was included as a within-participants factor. Chen et al. (2026) reported an overall medium effect of savoring interventions (Hedges' g = 0.51). In this study, a more conservative small effect (f = .10) was assumed for the power analysis. G*Power Version 3.1.9.6 (Faul et al., 2009) indicated that 200 participants were required for 80% power to detect the condition × time interaction at α = .05, assuming a repeated-measures correlation of .50.

prereg_check.title: Preregistration Check

table.title: Effects of finding and savoring kawaii on mood and prosocial behavior toward animals
table.research_questions:
Participants will be asked to view pictures of animals under one of two conditions: finding and savoring kawaii aspects of the animal (kawaii condition) or finding and describing the objective characteristics of the animal (objective condition).

H1: Participants in the kawaii condition will report higher (more positive) ratings for the pictures than those in the objective condition.

H2: Participants in the kawaii condition will show greater increases in positive mood and greater decreases in negative mood than those in the objective condition.

H3: Participants in the kawaii condition will show greater prosocial behavior toward animals than those in the objective condition.
table.foreknowledge_of_data_or_evidence: Data does not yet exist. No part of the data that will be used for this analysis plan exists, and no part will be generated until after this plan is registered.
table.study_type: Randomized Experiment: Must include random assignment of subjects to treatments or conditions. This usually includes lab experiments, field experiments, intervention experiments, randomized controlled trials, and A/B testing.
table.intention_for_causal_interpretation: Direct inference on causal relationship(s): This study is intended to infer or estimate a causal relationship between two or more variables. It is designed specifically for the purposes of causal inference or identification.
table.study_design_overview: The study uses a between-participants design with a factor of viewing condition (kawaii or objective). For mood outcomes, time (pre or post) will be included as a within-participants factor.
table.data_collection_procedures:
Adults aged 18 or older who find dogs and cats kawaii (cute) and have normal or corrected-to-normal vision will be recruited through a crowdsourcing service, Lancers (Tokyo, Japan). Participants will complete the experiment on their PC and provide open-ended responses in Japanese without using generative AI tools. The experiment will be conducted online using the Qualtrics platform (Seattle, WA, United States). Participants will be paid 300 Japanese yen for their participation (about 10–15 min).
Four animal pictures are used as stimuli: two dogs and two cats. The stimuli were selected from the Animal Affective Picture System (AAPS; Nittono & Nakamura, in preparation). In the AAPS, each picture has normative ratings for valence, arousal, motivational direction (approach–avoid), and kawaii (cuteness). For the present study, pictures were selected so that their ratings were close to the median values of the dog and cat pictures in the AAPS.
First, participants answer a questionnaire assessing their current mood. Then, they are instructed to view the following pictures in one of two ways: either to find and savor kawaii aspects of the animal, or to find and describe objective characteristics of the animal. In the picture viewing task, each trial begins with a preview of an animal picture for 3 s, followed by the viewing instruction. Participants then press a button to present the same picture again, which appears for 12 s. After viewing each picture, participants describe its kawaii aspects or objective characteristics freely and quantitatively rate the valence, arousal, motivational direction, kawaii, and willingness to care for it on 9-point scales. The order of animal pictures is randomized across participants.
After completing the picture viewing task, participants complete the mood questionnaire again. They are then offered an optional donation task related to animal support. If they choose to participate, they click a mouse button as many times as they wish within 5 s. Each click corresponds to a 1-Japanese-yen donation to an animal welfare organization, paid by the researcher. 
Finally, participants answer questions about how much they usually find dogs or cats kawaii and whether they have ever owned one or more. This study’s protocol was approved by the Behavioral Research Ethics Committee of the University of Osaka, School of Human Sciences, Japan (HB-R8-018), in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki.
table.sample_size_rationale: Chen et al. (2026) reported medium-sized effects of savoring interventions overall (Hedges’ g = 0.51) and on positive psychological states (Hedges’ g = 0.50). Because the present study uses a brief online task rather than a multi-day savoring intervention, a conservative small effect size (f = .10) was assumed for the power analysis. G*Power (Version 3.1.9.6) indicated that a total sample size of 200 would be needed to obtain 80% power to detect this effect at α = .05 for the within–between interaction in a 2 × 2 mixed ANOVA. The calculation assumed a correlation of .50 between repeated measures. To compensate for potential data loss due to incomplete responses or insufficient written descriptions, 300 participants will be recruited.
table.measured_variables:
1. Picture ratings: Valence, arousal, motivational direction, kawaii, and willingness to care for each animal picture.
2. Temporary Mood Scale (Tokuda, 2011): An 18-item, 5-point questionnaire with six subscales: Vigor, Tension, Depression, Anger, Confusion, and Fatigue (three items per subscale). 
3. Prosocial behavior: Participation rate in the donation task and the number of clicks.
4. Manipulation check: Understanding of their viewing task (i.e., goal) and the donation task (i.e., purpose, rules for determining amounts, and out-of-pocket cost).
5. Others: The degree to which participants usually find dogs or cats kawaii (5-point scales) and whether they have ever owned one or more.
table.indices: Temporary Mood Scale: Each subscale score will be calculated by summing up the three items. The Vigor score will be used as the positive mood score. The mean of the Tension, Depression, Anger, Confusion, and Fatigue subscale scores will be used as the negative mood score. These indices will be calculated separately before and after the picture viewing task.
table.statistical_tests:
H1 will be tested using linear mixed models for each picture rating score. Viewing condition (kawaii or objective) will be included as a fixed effect and participants and pictures as random effects.

H2 will be tested using 2 (viewing condition: kawaii or objective) × 2 (time: pre- or post-task) mixed ANOVA on the positive and negative mood scores.

H3 will be tested by comparing participation rates and the number of clicks in the mouse-click task between the two conditions. Participation rates will be compared using a chi-square test. The number of clicks will be compared using an independent samples t-test.
table.transformations: Number of clicks: Log transformed after adding 1.
table.inference_criteria: The significance level is set to .05 for all analyses.
table.data_exclusion_criteria:
The following participants will be excluded from the analyses:
1. Those who provide invalid descriptions, such as responses consisting only of meaningless strings (e.g., “aaaa”) or unrelated content.
2. Those who misunderstood the picture viewing and donation tasks.
3. Those who answer “not at all” to the questions about how much they usually find dogs and cats kawaii.
table.missing_data_handling: Participants with missing data will be excluded.
table.exploratory_analyses: Examine whether the two groups are similar in terms of how much participants usually find dogs or cats kawaii, as well as their experience with dog or cat ownership.

table.title: Effects of finding and savoring kawaii on mood and prosocial behavior toward animals (Experiment 2)
table.research_questions:
Participants will be asked to view pictures of animals under one of two conditions: finding and savoring kawaii aspects of the animal (kawaii condition) or finding and describing the objective characteristics of the animal (objective condition). 

The hypotheses are the same as those in Experiment 1.

H1: Participants in the kawaii condition will report higher (more positive) ratings for the pictures than those in the objective condition. 

H2: Participants in the kawaii condition will show greater increases in positive mood and greater decreases in negative mood than those in the objective condition. 

H3: Participants in the kawaii condition will show greater prosocial behavior toward animals than those in the objective condition.
table.foreknowledge_of_data_or_evidence: Data does not yet exist. No part of the data that will be used for this analysis plan exists, and no part will be generated until after this plan is registered.
table.study_type: Randomized Experiment: Must include random assignment of subjects to treatments or conditions. This usually includes lab experiments, field experiments, intervention experiments, randomized controlled trials, and A/B testing.
table.intention_for_causal_interpretation: Direct inference on causal relationship(s): This study is intended to infer or estimate a causal relationship between two or more variables. It is designed specifically for the purposes of causal inference or identification.
table.study_design_overview: The study uses a between-participants design with a factor of viewing condition (kawaii or objective). For mood outcomes, time (pre or post) will be included as a within-participants factor.
table.data_collection_procedures:
The data collection procedures are the same as in Experiment 1, except for the following:
(1) Adults who find animals, rather than dogs and cats, kawaii (cute) will be recruited.
(2) The free description duration per picture will be set at 90 s, which roughly corresponds to the mean duration in Experiment 1.
(3) Different animal pictures will be used: owl (7225.jpg), otter (6203.jpg), mouse (3242.jpg), and donkey (4235.jpg). These pictures have comparable valence, arousal, motivational direction, and kawaii ratings to those of the pictures used in Experiment 1.
(4) A Japanese version of the Positive and Negative Affect Schedule (PANAS; Sato & Yasuda, 2001) was used to assess mood, rather than the Temporary Mood Scale (TMS; Tokuda, 2011) used in Experiment 1.
table.sample_size: N = 200 each for male and female participants
table.sample_size_rationale: The sample size rationale is the same as in Experiment 1. To examine gender differences and to compensate for potential data loss due to incomplete responses or insufficient written descriptions, 250 male and 250 female participants will be recruited.
table.measured_variables:
1. Picture ratings: Valence, arousal, motivational direction, kawaii, and willingness to care for each animal picture. 
2. A Japanese version of the Positive and Negative Affect Schedule (PANAS; Sato & Yasuda, 2001): A 16-item, 6-point scale questionnaire with positive and negative subscales. 
3. Prosocial behavior: Participation rate in the donation task and the number of clicks. 
4. Manipulation check: Understanding of their viewing task (i.e., goal) and the donation task (i.e., purpose, rules for determining amounts, and out-of-pocket cost). 
5. Others: The subjective difficulty of the description task (1 = very easy, 5 = very difficult). The degree to which participants usually find animals kawaii (1 = not at all, 5 = very much) and whether they have ever owned one or more (Yes or No). Overall evaluation toward the feeling of kawaii (1 = very negative, 5 = very positive). Frequency of using the word “kawaii” in daily life (1 = not at all, 5 = very often).
table.indices: Positive and negative affect scores will be calculated according to the Japanese version of the PANAS (Sato & Yasuda, 2001). These scores will be calculated separately before and after the picture viewing task.
table.statistical_tests:
The statistical models are the same as in Experiment 1. 
H1 will be tested using linear mixed models for each picture rating score. Viewing condition (kawaii or objective) will be included as a fixed effect and participants and pictures as random effects. H2 will be tested using 2 (viewing condition: kawaii or objective) × 2 (time: pre- or post-task) mixed ANOVA on the positive and negative mood scores. H3 will be tested by comparing participation rates and the number of clicks in the mouse-click task between the two conditions. Participation rates will be compared using a chi-square test. The number of clicks will be compared using an independent samples t-test.
table.transformations: Number of clicks: Log transformed after adding 1.
table.inference_criteria: The significance level is set to .05 for all analyses.
table.data_exclusion_criteria: The following participants will be excluded from the analyses: 1. Those who provide invalid descriptions, such as responses consisting only of meaningless strings (e.g., “aaaa”) or unrelated content. 2. Those who misunderstood the picture viewing and donation tasks. 3. Those who answer “not at all” to the questions about how much they usually find animals kawaii.
table.missing_data_handling: Participants with missing data will be excluded.
table.exploratory_analyses:
Examine whether the two groups are similar in terms of how much participants usually find animals kawaii, as well as their experience with animal ownership.
An analysis of covariance (ANCOVA) will be performed on the change score, using the baseline (pre) positive or negative affect as a covariate.
table.randomization: Participants will be randomly assigned to one of two conditions. The animal pictures will be presented in a random order.

table.text: Exploratory ANCOVAs showed that higher pre-task positive mood was associated with smaller increases in positive mood, F(1, 279) = 24.15, p < .001, ηp² = .08.

table.text: After controlling for pre-task positive mood, the effect of viewing condition was significant, F(1, 279) = 4.56, p = .034, ηp² = .02.

table.text: However, the effect of viewing condition after controlling for pre-task negative mood was not significant, F(1, 279) = 0.79, p = .374, ηp² = .00.

Among participants who took part in the task (n = 237), log10-transformed click counts also did not differ between conditions (kawaii: M = 1.16, SD = 0.37; objective: M = 1.11, SD = 0.38), t(234.87) = 1.11, p = .269, d = 0.14.
The same conclusion was obtained for raw click counts (kawaii: M = 17.70, SD = 10.12; objective: M = 15.78, SD = 9.67), t(234.68) = 1.49, p = .137, d = 0.19.

#### Files that do not belong in the repository

We left out 7 files that software creates by itself, not the authors: operating system (7). They hold nothing a reader can use, but they clutter the repository, and software can mistake them for real files (for example a `._` copy of a `.csv` for data).

*Remove these:* *Operating system* files: macOS adds a `__MACOSX` folder and a `._` copy of every file it puts in a zip, and `.DS_Store` files to folders; Windows adds `Thumbs.db` and `desktop.ini`. On a Mac, create zips from the command line with `zip -r -X`, or remove them afterwards with `zip -d archive.zip "__MACOSX/*" "*.DS_Store"`. *RStudio session files* (`.Rproj.user/`) hold open tabs and unsaved edits; *R history* (`.Rhistory`) lists the commands typed in a session and can hold file paths and passwords; *Jupyter checkpoints* (`.ipynb_checkpoints/`) are automatic copies of notebooks; *compiled Python files* (`__pycache__/`, `.pyc`) are recreated when the code runs; *open-document lock files* (`~$...docx`, `.~lock...#`) are left while a document is open; *editor backups* (`file~`, `.bak`, `.swp`) and *temporary files* (`.tmp`, `.temp`) are copies a program made by itself.

*Keep only on purpose:* *version control* folders (`.git`, `.svn`, `.hg`) hold the project's history, which can include earlier versions of files and data that was later removed; *editor settings* (`.idea`, `.vscode`) can hold paths on your own computer. A `.gitignore` based on GitHub's templates (https://github.com/github/gitignore) keeps them out of a repository.

#### Spreadsheet Formatting
We examined 1 spreadsheet file in the repository; 1 has at least one formatting issue.

Spreadsheet formatting such as colour, merged cells, and blank rows/columns is not preserved when data are read programmatically or exported to CSV. Store data as a plain rectangular table (one header row, one column per variable, no colour-encoded meaning) so it is machine-readable.

Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

reproducibility_check.title: Reproducibility Check
reproducibility_check.summary_text:
-  We assessed AND ran 1 R code file for reproducibility (each in an isolated Docker container).
-  1 of 1 script ran without error when executed.
-  2 installable dependencies detected.
- 2119 statistics stored from the extracted output; 52 of 71 reported tests matched (73.2%).

summary_table.ethics_statements: Experiment 1 was approved by the Behavioral Research Ethics Committee of the University of Osaka, School of Human Sciences, Japan (HB-R8-018) in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki.
live_data_statements: Participants were instructed to try to look for the kawaii aspects of animal pictures and to savor the positive feelings that arose from doing so.

G*Power Version 3.1.9.6 (Faul et al., 2009) indicated that 200 participants were required for 80% power to detect the condition × time interaction at α = .05, assuming a repeated-measures correlation of .50.
A total of 300 participants were recruited through a crowdsourcing service (Lancers, Tokyo, Japan) to compensate for potential data loss.
Participants were adults aged 18 years or older who had experienced feelings of kawaii toward dogs or cats, had normal
First, the participants completed the mood questionnaire and then performed the picture-viewing task.

In the kawaii condition, participants were instructed to find the kawaii aspects of each animal and experience the resulting feeling of kawaii, whereas those in the objective condition were instructed to identify its objective characteristics.
After completing the viewing task, the participants completed the mood questionnaire again.

After reading a text about the situation of sheltered dogs and cats in Japan (see Table S1 for the full text), the participants were offered an optional donation task in which each mouse click within 5 s resulted in a 1-yen donation by the researcher to an animal welfare organization.
Based on the preregistered exclusion criteria, 18 participants were excluded for failing the instruction-comprehension check (n = 9) or the comprehension checks for the donation task (n = 9).

To address these issues, the following changes were made in Experiment 2: (1) a standard description time of 90 s was set; (2) different animals than dogs and cats were used; (3) mood was assessed with the Japanese version of the Positive and Negative Affect Schedule (PANAS; Watson et al., 1988; Sato & Yasuda, 2001); and (4) approximately equal numbers of men and women were recruited.

Participants were excluded for failing the instruction-comprehension check (n = 41) or donation-task comprehension checks (n = 24), or for reporting that they never found animals kawaii (n = 1); one participant met both of the first two criteria.
No participant provided invalid free descriptions.
Participants completed the experiment online on their own PCs using Qualtrics (Seattle, WA, United States) and were paid 300 Japanese yen.
All participants provided electronic informed consent online.

report: This module assesses whether the paper's code could be run on its data, and — because `execute = TRUE` — **actually ran it**. We examined 1 R code file.
#### Run order
The scripts were ordered by their data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads runs first), `source()` calls, and numeric filename prefixes.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(Order = 1L, File = "analysis.R", "Runs after" = "—", 
    Basis = "none"), row.names = c(NA, -1L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```
#### File paths
Every data path in the code works in the repository as deposited.
#### Execution

**The code was run.** Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 1 script: 1 ran without error, 0 errored, 0 timed out, 0 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions.

text.text: The Japanese word 'kawaii' describes not only an object's cute attributes but also a positive feeling toward it.
Although viewing cute objects can improve mood and encourage prosocial behavior, it remains unclear whether intentionally focusing on kawaii feelings enhances these effects.
In two online experiments, participants viewed pictures of dogs and cats (N = 282) and other animals (N = 435).
They were instructed to either find and savor the kawaii aspects of the animals or to find and describe their objective characteristics.
The results showed that the picture ratings of valence, arousal, approach motivation, and kawaii were higher in the kawaii condition than in the objective condition.
However, no significant differences were found between the conditions in terms of mood change or donation-related voluntary actions.
Focusing on kawaii aspects can improve affective evaluation, but a one-time savoring session may not be sufficient to alter mood or behavior.
People are frequently exposed to cute content in their daily lives, particularly on social media (Golonka et al., 2023).
text.formatted: People are frequently exposed to cute content in their daily lives, particularly on social media <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Golonka et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Research has shown that cute pictures are rated as more pleasant and elicit stronger smiling responses than neutral pictures (Nittono & Ihara, 2017).
text.formatted: Research has shown that cute pictures are rated as more pleasant and elicit stronger smiling responses than neutral pictures <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Nittono & Ihara, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: They are also associated with feelings of healing (Chou et al., 2022) or kama muta, a heartwarming feeling of being moved (Steinnes et al., 2019). Myrick (2015) surveyed 6,795 internet users and suggested that people may watch cat videos and look at cat pictures, which are often described as cute, as an easily accessible means of emotion regulation.

text.text: However, it remains unclear whether these positive responses are automatically triggered by mere exposure or they can be intentionally enhanced by changing the way people view these stimuli.
The research on cuteness has started with the concept of Kindernschema (baby schema).
In his seminal monograph, Lorenz (1943) suggested that infantile features, such as a large head, rounded body, and chubby cheeks, elicit positive feelings and caregiving behavior.
text.formatted: In his seminal monograph, <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Lorenz (1943)</ref> suggested that infantile features, such as a large head, rounded body, and chubby cheeks, elicit positive feelings and caregiving behavior.

text.text: These features have been shown to increase perceived cuteness and caregiving motivation (Glocker et al., 2009) and activate reward-related brain regions (Kringelbach et al., 2008).

text.text: Despite its intuitive appeal, the concept of baby schema has been inconsistently used, and its evolutionary significance remains unclear (Kawaguchi & Waller, 2024). Garsmeur and Baumard (2026) recently proposed that cuteness motivates developmental investment in inexperienced individuals beyond mere protection.

text.text: The present study focuses on the feelings evoked by cute objects rather than on their physical features.

While the English word 'cuteness' mainly refers to an object's physical and perceptual attributes (Buckley, 2016), the Japanese concept of 'kawaii' includes both these attributes and the feelings evoked in the perceiver (Nittono, 2016; Nittono et al., 2023).

text.text: In the latter sense, kawaii can be understood as a subjective emotional experience arising from cognitive appraisal and associated with approach motivation, such as wanting to get closer, keep watching, and care for the object (Nittono, 2016).

text.text: Throughout this article, the term kawaii is used to include this emotional aspect.
Recent studies have suggested that perceived cuteness is shaped not only by physical features but also by cognitive factors.

Cuteness ratings can change through perceptual adaptation (Golle et al., 2013), familiarization (Hunt et al., 2023; Hunt & De Pascalis, 2024), and the objects' temperament (Parsons et al., 2014) and personality description (Takamatsu et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Cuteness ratings can change through perceptual adaptation <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Golle et al., 2013)</ref>, familiarization <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Hunt et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Hunt & De Pascalis, 2024)</ref>, and the objects' temperament <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Parsons et al., 2014)</ref> and personality description <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">(Takamatsu et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: For example, Takamatsu et al. (2023) found that pairing children's faces with positive personality descriptions increased perceived cuteness, whereas negative descriptions decreased it, and these changes in cuteness mediated the effects of the descriptions on nurturing motivation.

(2023)</ref> found that pairing children's faces with positive personality descriptions increased perceived cuteness, whereas negative descriptions decreased it, and these changes in cuteness mediated the effects of the descriptions on nurturing motivation.

text.text: Contextual information, knowledge, and experience can influence perceived cuteness, even when an object's physical features remain unchanged.

Psychological responses to cuteness-related stimuli can change depending on how they are evaluated. Nittono and Ohashi (2024) found that smiling-related facial muscle activity was stronger when participants rated the cuteness rather than the beauty of infant faces. Turner-Collins and Breitenbecher (2019) showed that evaluating dogs on humanlike rather than canine traits reduced subsequent pain intensity in the presence of a therapy dog.

text.text: These examples suggest that changing the way people view a stimulus may alter its consequences.

One way to change the perspective is by savoring (Bryant, 1989), which involves intentionally attending to and appreciating positive experiences to enhance and maintain positive emotions (Bryant, 2021; Bryant et al., 2011).
text.formatted: One way to change the perspective is by savoring <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Bryant, 1989)</ref>, which involves intentionally attending to and appreciating positive experiences to enhance and maintain positive emotions <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Bryant, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Bryant et al., 2011)</ref>.

text.text: Experimental studies have shown that savoring can enhance evaluations of positive stimuli and emotional well-being (see Chen et al., 2026, for a recent review). Wilson and MacNamara (2021) found that focusing on the positive aspects of pictures increased their pleasantness ratings, with the effect persisting when the pictures were later viewed without savoring instructions.

text.text: Such prosocial effects of cute stimuli may reflect broader human sociality rather than caregiving alone (Sherman & Haidt, 2011).

text.text: Cute stimuli may promote prosocial behavior through the positive feeling of kawaii, since positive affect facilitates prosociality (Lyubomirsky et al., 2005).

text.text: If finding and savoring kawaii aspects of animals increases positive affect, it may promote prosocial behavior toward animals.

This study examined whether finding and savoring kawaii aspects of animal pictures improves affective ratings of the pictures, momentary mood, and prosocial behavior toward animals, compared with finding and describing their objective characteristics.
Participants were instructed to try to look for the kawaii aspects of animal pictures and to savor the positive feelings that arose from doing so.
Animals were selected because they are typical cute stimuli (Borgi et al., 2014) and have been used in previous research on savoring (Wilson & MacNamara, 2024).
text.formatted: Animals were selected because they are typical cute stimuli <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Borgi et al., 2014)</ref> and have been used in previous research on savoring <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">(Wilson & MacNamara, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: The click-donation task (Takamatsu & Nittono, in press) was used to test the effect on prosocial behavior.
text.formatted: The click-donation task <ref type="bibr">(Takamatsu & Nittono, in press</ref>) was used to test the effect on prosocial behavior.

text.text: There were three hypotheses: Participants in the kawaii condition would report more positive picture ratings (H1), greater increases in positive mood and decreases in negative mood (H2), and greater prosocial behavior toward animals (H3) than those in the objective condition.
The experiments were preregistered: Experiments 1 (https://osf.io/b7wpz/) and 2 (https://osf.io/e4qt8/).

For mood outcomes, time (pre-or post-task) was included as a within-participants factor. Chen et al. (2026) reported an overall medium effect of savoring interventions (Hedges' g = 0.51).

Four animal pictures (two dogs: 1044.jpg, 1079.jpg; two cats: 2009.jpg, 2100.jpg) were selected from the Animal Affective Picture System (AAPS; Nittono & Nakamura, 2026), which provides normative 9-point ratings (1-9) of valence, arousal, motivational direction (approach-avoidance), and kawaii (cuteness).
text.formatted: Four animal pictures (two dogs: 1044.jpg, 1079.jpg; two cats: 2009.jpg, 2100.jpg) were selected from the Animal Affective Picture System (AAPS; <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Nittono & Nakamura, 2026)</ref>, which provides normative 9-point ratings (1-9) of valence, arousal, motivational direction (approach-avoidance), and kawaii (cuteness).

text.text: To avoid ceiling and floor effects, pictures were selected with ratings close to the median values of the 225 dog and cat pictures in the AAPS.
The mean ratings of the selected pictures were 6.38, 4.88, 6.42, and 6.59, for valence, arousal, motivational direction, and kawaii, respectively.
All animals faced forward, and both eyes were visible.
Picture rating.

Each picture was rated for valence, arousal, motivational direction, kawaii, and willingness to care for the animal (hereinafter, willingness to care) on 9point scales (valence:1 = very negative,5 = neutral,9 = very positive; arousal:1 = calm,5 = neutral,9 = excited; motivational direction:1 = to avoid,5 = neutral,9 = to approach; kawaii:1 = not at all kawaii,9 = extremely kawaii; willingness to care:1 = not at all,9 = very much).
Mood questionnaire.

Mood was assessed using the Temporary Mood Scale (Tokuda, 2011), which consists of six three-item subscales (tension, depression, anger, confusion, fatigue, and vigor) rated on a 5-point scale (1 = not at all applicable,5 = very applicable).

text.text: In the present study, Cronbach's α calculated separately for pre-and posttask ratings ranged from .86 to .88 for vigor and from .70 to .92 for the five negative mood subscales, comparable to previously reported values (α = .78-.87; Tokuda, 2007).

text.text: The sum of the three vigor items was used as the positive mood index, and the mean of the summed scores of the other five subscales was used as the negative mood index (ranges: 3-15).

text.text: First, the participants completed the mood questionnaire and then performed the picture-viewing task.

In the kawaii condition, participants were instructed to find the kawaii aspects of each animal and experience the resulting feeling of kawaii, whereas those in the objective condition were instructed to identify its objective characteristics.
Both groups then described the identified aspects in writing.
The full instructions are provided in Table S1.
text.formatted: The full instructions are provided in Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">S1</ref>.

text.text: Each trial began with a preview of an animal picture for 3 s, followed by viewing instructions and presentation of the same picture for 12 s.
Participants then described its kawaii aspects or objective characteristics and rated the picture for valence, arousal, motivational direction, kawaii, and willingness to care.
The four pictures were presented in random order.
After completing the viewing task, the participants completed the mood questionnaire again.

After reading a text about the situation of sheltered dogs and cats in Japan (see Table S1 for the full text), the participants were offered an optional donation task in which each mouse click within 5 s resulted in a 1-yen donation by the researcher to an animal welfare organization.

text.text: They then reported how they had viewed the pictures to check their understanding of the task.
Finally, they rated how kawaii they usually found dogs and cats separately (1 = not at all kawaii,5 = very kawaii) and reported whether they had ever owned a dog or a cat.

H1 was tested using linear mixed models for each picture rating, with viewing condition (kawaii or objective) as a fixed effect and participants and pictures as random effects: rating ~ viewing condition + (1 | participant) + (1 | picture).
Fixed effects were tested using Type III sums of squares with Satterthwaite's degrees of freedom.
H2 was tested using a 2 (viewing condition: kawaii or objective) × 2 (time: pre-or post-task) mixed ANOVA on the positive and negative mood scores.
H3 was tested by comparing donation-task participation rates using a chi-square test and, among those who participated, the number of clicks using Welch's t-test.
Following Takamatsu and Nittono (in press), click counts were log10-transformed after adding 1, and the analysis was repeated using raw scores.

Experiment 1 showed that finding and savoring kawaii aspects of animal pictures increased all five picture ratings.
These findings suggest that focusing on different aspects of an object can modify subjective evaluations.
However, finding and savoring kawaii aspects did not improve post-task mood or prosocial behavior.
Experiment 1 had several limitations.
First, participants in the kawaii condition spent less time on free description than those in the objective condition, so differences in task duration may have influenced the results.
Second, dogs and cats are typical companion animals (Pongrácz & Dobos, 2023), and it remained unclear whether the effects would generalize to less familiar species.
text.formatted: Second, dogs and cats are typical companion animals <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(Pongrácz & Dobos, 2023)</ref>, and it remained unclear whether the effects would generalize to less familiar species.

text.text: Third, the mood questionnaire had a significant disparity in the number of positive and negative items: three for positive mood and 15 for negative mood.
Fourth, the sample included about twice as many men as women.

To address these issues, the following changes were made in Experiment 2: (1) a standard description time of 90 s was set; (2) different animals than dogs and cats were used; (3) mood was assessed with the Japanese version of the Positive and Negative Affect Schedule (PANAS; Watson et al., 1988; Sato & Yasuda, 2001); and (4) approximately equal numbers of men and women were recruited.

text.text: The main effect of time was significant for both positive and negative affect, with positive affect increasing and negative affect decreasing from pre-to post-task.

Neither the main effect of viewing condition nor the condition × time interaction was significant (ps > .069), although the increase in positive affect (range: -40 to +40) was descriptively larger in the kawaii condition (M = 1.15) than in the objective condition (M = 0.28).
text.formatted: Neither the main effect of viewing condition nor the condition × time interaction was significant (ps > .069), although the increase in positive affect (range: -40 to +40) was descriptively larger in the kawaii condition (M = 1.15) than in the objective condition (M = 0.28).

text.text: Exploratory ANCOVAs showed significant effects of pre-task mood on both positive affect change, F(1, 432) = 19.22, p < .001, ηp² = .04, and negative affect change, F(1, 432) = 182.10, p < .001, ηp² = .30.
text.formatted: Exploratory ANCOVAs showed significant effects of pre-task mood on both positive affect change, F(1, 432) = 19.22, p < .001, ηp² = .04, and negative affect change, F(1, 432) = 182.10, p < .001, ηp² = .30.

text.text: After controlling for pre-task mood, viewing condition did not significantly affect either positive or negative affect change (ps > .105).
text.formatted: After controlling for pre-task mood, viewing condition did not significantly affect either positive or negative affect change (ps > .105).

text.text: Donation-task participation did not differ between the kawaii (175/222, 78.8%) and objective conditions (169/213, 79.3%), χ 2 (1) = 0.02, p = .895.

Among the participants who took part in the task (n = 344), log10-transformed click counts also did not differ between conditions (kawaii: M = 1.02, SD = 0.42; objective: M = 1.07, SD = 0.35), t(334.69) = 1.18, p = .239, d = 0.13.
The same conclusion was obtained for raw click counts (kawaii: M = 13.87, SD = 10.08; objective: M = 14.19, SD = 9.12), t(340.60) = 0.31, p = .757, d = 0.03.
Experiment 2 was conducted to replicate the findings of Experiment 1 by addressing several technical concerns.

Similar to Experiment 1, finding and savoring the kawaii aspects of animal pictures increased ratings of valence, arousal, motivational direction, and kawaii ratings, with a similar tendency for willingness to care.
This suggests that the effect was not limited to dogs and cats.
The weaker effect on willingness to care may be because the animals used in Experiment 2 were less likely to be perceived as care targets than dogs and cats (Possidónio et al., 2019).
text.formatted: The weaker effect on willingness to care may be because the animals used in Experiment 2 were less likely to be perceived as care targets than dogs and cats <ref type="bibr">(Possidónio et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Effects on mood and prosocial behavior were not observed again.
The effect on positive mood change found in Experiment 1 after controlling for pre-task mood was not replicated.
No condition differences were found in donation-task participation or the number of clicks.

Across the two experiments, finding and savoring the kawaii aspects of animal pictures increased picture ratings, supporting H1, whereas no clear effects were found on mood (H2) or prosocial behavior (H3).

Finding kawaii aspects of animal pictures and savoring the evoked feelings enhanced evaluations of the pictures in both experiments, consistent with findings that focusing on positive aspects of pictures increases their ratings (Wilson & MacNamara, 2021 , 2024).
text.formatted: Finding kawaii aspects of animal pictures and savoring the evoked feelings enhanced evaluations of the pictures in both experiments, consistent with findings that focusing on positive aspects of pictures increases their ratings <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">(Wilson & MacNamara, 2021</ref> <ref type="bibr">, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Because 'kawaii' and 'cute' have positive connotations (Nittono, 2016; Nittono et al., 2021), the instruction to find kawaii aspects is virtually the same as focusing on the positive aspects of the pictures.
text.formatted: Because 'kawaii' and 'cute' have positive connotations <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Nittono, 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Nittono et al., 2021)</ref>, the instruction to find kawaii aspects is virtually the same as focusing on the positive aspects of the pictures.

text.text: Higher kawaii ratings in the kawaii condition may partly reflect demand characteristics.
However, valence and approach motivation ratings also increased, despite not being mentioned in the instructions.

This pattern agrees with kawaii as a positive emotion associated with approach motivation (Nittono, 2016), suggesting that finding kawaii aspects influences broader affective and motivational evaluations.
text.formatted: This pattern agrees with kawaii as a positive emotion associated with approach motivation <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Nittono, 2016)</ref>, suggesting that finding kawaii aspects influences broader affective and motivational evaluations.

text.text: While previous research has primarily examined physical features that make stimuli cute (e.g., Aradhye et al., 2015; Borgi et al., 2014; Yao et al., 2022), the present findings show that viewing the same stimulus from different perspectives can also shape responses to it.
text.formatted: While previous research has primarily examined physical features that make stimuli cute (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">Aradhye et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">Borgi et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">Yao et al., 2022)</ref>, the present findings show that viewing the same stimulus from different perspectives can also shape responses to it.

text.text: Task difficulty provides an alternative explanation.

Easier processing can produce more positive evaluations (Alter & Oppenheimer, 2009), and the objective task appeared more difficult; participants spent more time on free description in Experiment 1 and rated the task as more difficult in Experiment 2.
text.formatted: Easier processing can produce more positive evaluations <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Alter & Oppenheimer, 2009)</ref>, and the objective task appeared more difficult; participants spent more time on free description in Experiment 1 and rated the task as more difficult in Experiment 2.

text.text: Task difficulty may have contributed to the condition differences in picture ratings.
Positive mood increased and negative mood decreased after viewing animal pictures, but the effect of kawaii and objective conditions on mood change was not significant.
The mood improvement may be partly due to viewing cute animal pictures (Myrick, 2015).
text.formatted: The mood improvement may be partly due to viewing cute animal pictures <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Myrick, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: However, simply viewing animal pictures does not necessarily improve mood (Machová & Flegr, 2025).
text.formatted: However, simply viewing animal pictures does not necessarily improve mood <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Machová & Flegr, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Although there was no passive-viewing condition in this study, the improvement may result from the active processing of the pictures required in both conditions.

Although the increase in positive mood was descriptively larger in the kawaii condition in both experiments, the lack of significant interactions suggests that the effect of finding and savoring kawaii on mood was small.
The objective condition also required close attention to potentially positive (cute) stimuli and may thus have shared some features of savoring.
In a meta-analysis paper, Chen et al. (2026) mentioned that the effect of savoring interventions is smaller when compared to active control conditions than passive control conditions.
text.formatted: In a meta-analysis paper, <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Chen et al. (2026)</ref> mentioned that the effect of savoring interventions is smaller when compared to active control conditions than passive control conditions.

text.text: Unlike previous studies using neutral stimuli or different control tasks (e.g., Klibert et al., 2022; Rosen & LaFreniere, 2023), the present conditions differed mainly in the perspective from which the pictures were viewed.
text.formatted: Unlike previous studies using neutral stimuli or different control tasks (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Klibert et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Rosen & LaFreniere, 2023)</ref>, the present conditions differed mainly in the perspective from which the pictures were viewed.

text.text: These task features may have limited the observed effect of savoring kawaii on mood.
Previous studies have shown that cuteness promotes donation intentions (Baek et al., 2025; Phan et al., 2026) and donation-related behavior (Takamatsu & Nittono, in press).
text.formatted: Previous studies have shown that cuteness promotes donation intentions <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Baek et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Phan et al., 2026)</ref> and donation-related behavior <ref type="bibr">(Takamatsu & Nittono, in press</ref>).

text.text: In the present study, however, no significant differences in donation behavior were found between conditions.

In their scoping review, Thomas-Walters et al. ( 2020)suggested that showing animal images can promote viewers' protective attitudes toward the animals, particularly when they find the animals aesthetically pleasing.
text.formatted: In their scoping review, Thomas-Walters et al. ( <ref type="formula">2020)</ref>suggested that showing animal images can promote viewers' protective attitudes toward the animals, particularly when they find the animals aesthetically pleasing.

text.text: However, this does not always result in actual behavior.
Considering that positive mood can promote prosocial behavior (Lyubomirsky et al., 2005), the lack of a mood difference between conditions may partly explain the absence of an effect on donations.
text.formatted: Considering that positive mood can promote prosocial behavior <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Lyubomirsky et al., 2005)</ref>, the lack of a mood difference between conditions may partly explain the absence of an effect on donations.

text.text: In addition, whereas participants in Takamatsu and Nittono (in press) donated to help the pictured animals, the present donation task concerned sheltered animals in general.
text.formatted: In addition, whereas participants in <ref type="bibr">Takamatsu and Nittono (in press</ref>) donated to help the pictured animals, the present donation task concerned sheltered animals in general.

text.text: Given the increased willingness to care for the animals, the effects of finding kawaii aspects may have been specific to the animals actually viewed rather than other animals in general.
Perceiving and savoring kawaii may produce short-term effects on responses toward concrete targets rather than influencing general prosociality.
This study has several limitations.
First, the Japanese sample limits cultural generalizability.

Because Japanese kawaii encompasses both object characteristics and perceivers' positive feelings and is used more broadly than comparable English and Spanish terms (Nittono et al., 2023), future studies should examine whether savoring kawaii is also effective in different cultures.
text.formatted: Because Japanese kawaii encompasses both object characteristics and perceivers' positive feelings and is used more broadly than comparable English and Spanish terms <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Nittono et al., 2023)</ref>, future studies should examine whether savoring kawaii is also effective in different cultures.

text.text: Second, only animal pictures were used.

Because savoring effects were generalized to novel animal pictures but not people pictures (Wilson & MacNamara, 2024), and kawaii pictures with and without baby schema elicited partly different responses (Nittono & Ihara, 2017), future studies should examine whether similar effects occur for other kawaii stimuli, such as infants and objects.
text.formatted: Because savoring effects were generalized to novel animal pictures but not people pictures <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">(Wilson & MacNamara, 2024)</ref>, and kawaii pictures with and without baby schema elicited partly different responses <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Nittono & Ihara, 2017)</ref>, future studies should examine whether similar effects occur for other kawaii stimuli, such as infants and objects.

text.text: Third, it is unclear whether the participants actually savored the evoked feelings.
The instructions encouraged participants to experience kawaii but not explicitly to attend to and maintain the feelings, which are central to savoring (Bryant, 2021; Bryant & Veroff, 2007).
text.formatted: The instructions encouraged participants to experience kawaii but not explicitly to attend to and maintain the feelings, which are central to savoring <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Bryant, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Bryant & Veroff, 2007)</ref>.

text.text: Previous brief interventions have involved attending to positive stimuli or memories and their evoked feelings for 10-15 min, which was longer than in this study (Klibert et al., 2022; B. A. Wang et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Previous brief interventions have involved attending to positive stimuli or memories and their evoked feelings for 10-15 min, which was longer than in this study <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Klibert et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">B. A. Wang et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Furthermore, verbalizing positive experiences may be less beneficial than imagining or replaying them (Holmes et al., 2006; Lyubomirsky et al., 2006).
text.formatted: Furthermore, verbalizing positive experiences may be less beneficial than imagining or replaying them <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Holmes et al., 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Lyubomirsky et al., 2006)</ref>.

text.text: Future studies should use more explicit savoring instructions and assess the extent of savoring and the duration of positive feelings (e.g., Rosen & LaFreniere, 2023).
text.formatted: Future studies should use more explicit savoring instructions and assess the extent of savoring and the duration of positive feelings (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Rosen & LaFreniere, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Fourth, no passive control condition was included.
Such a condition would help determine whether the mood improvement observed in both conditions resulted from merely viewing the pictures or from actively processing them.

The two experiments consistently showed that the instruction to find and savor kawaii aspects of animal pictures enhanced participants' evaluations of these pictures, but it did not reliably influence mood or prosocial behavior.

Since people like cute things and the feeling of kawaii depends not only on stimulus characteristics but also on how people view the stimulus, this "savoring kawaii" approach is easily applicable to everyday situations and is a potentially useful way of emotional regulation.

Responses to animal pictures may depend on viewers' characteristics.
People who usually find animals kawaii may rate animal pictures more positively and be more willing to care for animals.
Pet ownership is associated with positive attitudes toward animals (Auger & Amiot, 2017) and more positive ratings of animal pictures (Possidónio et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Pet ownership is associated with positive attitudes toward animals <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">(Auger & Amiot, 2017)</ref> and more positive ratings of animal pictures <ref type="bibr">(Possidónio et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: The present analyses examined whether general kawaii feelings, previous ownership, and gender were related to the outcomes and moderated the effects of the viewing instructions.

Previous ownership was expected to be associated with higher general kawaii feelings, and both were expected to be positively associated with picture ratings, mood improvement, and prosocial behavior.
Gender was examined exploratorily.
The association between previous ownership and general kawaii feelings toward animals was first examined.
General kawaii feelings were indexed by the mean of the ratings for dogs and cats in Experiment 1 and by a single rating for animals in general in Experiment 2.

ANCOVAs were then conducted on the picture ratings, mood change scores, and the number of clicks, with viewing condition, general kawaii feelings, previous ownership, gender, and the interactions of viewing condition with each of these variables.
Continuous variables were mean-centered, and binary variables were coded using weighted effect coding to account for unequal group sizes (te Grotenhuis et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Continuous variables were mean-centered, and binary variables were coded using weighted effect coding to account for unequal group sizes <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">(te Grotenhuis et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Participation in the donation task was analyzed using logistic regression with the same predictors.
Participants with previous pet ownership reported higher general kawaii feelings toward animals than those without (Experiment 1: r = .24; Experiment 2: r = .27; ps < .001).
text.formatted: Participants with previous pet ownership reported higher general kawaii feelings toward animals than those without (Experiment 1: r = .24; Experiment 2: r = .27; ps < .001).

text.text: After controlling for the individual difference variables, the effects of viewing condition on all five picture ratings were significant in both experiments (Table S5), including willingness to care in Experiment 2, which was not significant in the preregistered analysis.
text.formatted: After controlling for the individual difference variables, the effects of viewing condition on all five picture ratings were significant in both experiments (Table <ref type="table">S5</ref>), including willingness to care in Experiment 2, which was not significant in the preregistered analysis.

text.text: The effects of viewing condition on mood change, the number of clicks, and donation-task participation remained nonsignificant (Tables S6-S8).
text.formatted: The effects of viewing condition on mood change, the number of clicks, and donation-task participation remained nonsignificant (Tables <ref type="table">S6-S8</ref>).

text.text: Participants with higher general kawaii feelings gave higher picture ratings, showed greater increases in positive mood, made more clicks, and were more likely to participate in the donation task in both experiments.
They also showed a greater decrease in negative mood in Experiment 1 only.
Previous ownership was related only to fewer clicks in Experiment 1.
In Experiment 1, women gave higher valence, arousal, and kawaii ratings and showed a greater decrease in negative mood than men; gender was not related to any outcome in Experiment 2.
Interactions between viewing condition and the individual difference variables were mostly nonsignificant, and none of the significant interactions was replicated across the two experiments.

General kawaii feelings toward animals were related to most of the outcome variables, and controlling for these individual differences did not change the effects of viewing condition on picture ratings.
As expected, previous ownership was associated with higher general kawaii feelings but was largely unrelated to the outcomes.
The higher picture ratings by pet owners in previous research (Possidónio et al., 2019) may therefore partly reflect their general kawaii feelings.
text.formatted: The higher picture ratings by pet owners in previous research <ref type="bibr">(Possidónio et al., 2019)</ref> may therefore partly reflect their general kawaii feelings.

text.text: Across both experiments, general kawaii feelings toward animals, rather than previous ownership or gender, were consistently related to responses to the animal pictures and donation behavior.
